OpenAI’s IPO Countdown Clock Is Ticking
 
Plus, Jensen Huang is back, and Anthropic is marching toward profitability
 
 
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. SPENCER PLATT/GETTY IMAGES
 

Last week, OpenAI was in the odd position of rooting for the success of its fiercest competitor’s IPO. This week, the focus will turn to when OpenAI follows suit—or if market turbulence derails an offering for the foreseeable future.

 

There have always been good reasons for OpenAI to move quickly. While IPO timing isn’t a big determinant of long-term business success, there are clear advantages in being a first mover.

 

Back in 2019, for instance, Lyft rushed to an IPO faster than its ride-sharing rival Uber. But Lyft’s listing got off to a rocky start, which impacted the initial pricing of Uber’s shares.

 

Uber ultimately fared much better than its rival—its market capitalization is about $130 billion, compared with about $6 billion for Lyft. But early on, Uber’s decision to wait looked like a mistake.

 

For OpenAI, the factor that matters most is the health of the AI market that it is a central part of. The company’s current plan is to wait until next year, which makes some sense from an operational standpoint.

 
 
 
CONTENT FROM: PWC
 
 
We Turn AI Noise Into AI Solutions
 
Everyone is talking about AI. But is any of it actually working for your business? At PwC, we help cut through the AI noise so you can solve the problems that matter.
 
Learn More  >
 
 
 

OpenAI, after all, has been bleeding executive talent this year. Its financial condition doesn’t look stellar when compared with Anthropic’s, either. OpenAI’s revenue grew by 50% from the second quarter to the third, reaching $10 billion. But Anthropic’s grew to $17 billion in the same period, while it reported a smaller operating loss than OpenAI.

 

OpenAI and its board may want time to build a better financial case to present to investors. If OpenAI is able to gain a step on Anthropic in model development and take some of its market share in sales of AI tools to companies, its story becomes more compelling.

 

At the same time, every minute that ticks away exposes OpenAI further to another risk: That the wheels come off the AI trade.

 

Should that happen, history suggests the window for OpenAI to list might close for a long time. IPOs dried up for a few years following the 1987 crash, the dot-com bust and the financial crisis, said Jay Ritter, an economist and director of The IPO Initiative at the University of Florida’s business school.

 

“I don’t see a compelling reason to wait more than a couple months,” he said.

 

At the moment, markets don’t look too inviting for another big IPO, even with Monday’s rebound in tech stocks. Anthropic’s shares are now below their IPO price, having fallen on Monday and into Tuesday even as other tech shares fared better.

 

Despite all that, the reasons for OpenAI to move with some urgency are fairly overwhelming, given how much funding it wants to fuel its ambitions. The company plans to spend around $750 billion through 2030 on computing power to develop its AI models. Being publicly listed gives it tools essential to accomplish that, and there is no telling how much longer the markets’ AI party can last.

 

This is an edition of the WSJ AI & Business newsletter, a weekly digest to help you make sense of AI’s impact on business with news, insights and data from our global team of technology journalists. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

He’s Back

 
 
JASON HENRY FOR WSJ
 

Jensen Huang made a Sam Altman-esque return on Monday, resuming his role as chief executive of Nvidia after an 11-day hiatus. The stunning about-face by Nvidia’s board, which only last week said it wasn’t considering reappointing Huang, sent Nvidia’s shares skyrocketing in trading on Monday. There remain many questions, however, about how the company moves beyond national-security concerns about Huang, as well as how the chief executive’s return might affect its financial support for the AI ecosystem.

 
 
 

The Number

 
167 Years
 

Time since Bernhard Riemann proposed a seminal mathematical hypothesis that an Anthropic researcher claimed to have solved using AI last week.

 
 
 

What the Humans Are Saying

 

“The tentacles of AI are remarkable.”

 

— Jonathan Pingle, UBS economist, on the reach of the AI boom in the broader economy.

 
 
 

AI in Charts

 
 
 
 

Anthropic is a money-losing company. But it is on a trajectory to eventually turn a profit.

 

Anthropic’s march toward profitability as its operating margins expand is one reason why betting on it isn’t totally irrational—even if its capital spending plans look bonkers and its ability to raise enough money at low-enough interest rates is questionable.

 

That upward march also underlines the business sense behind Anthropic’s sales and development strategy. Untold numbers of corporations see value in using AI tools to save money and simply move faster. Anthropic has catered to them, making companies its core customers rather than trying to convince consumers to pay for AI.

 

In some ways, that focus could be a growing challenge in the future: Anthropic is competing with already very profitable heavyweights like Google for corporate customers. Yet Anthropic is unencumbered by the massive franchises tech companies have built up over the years—an edge that should make it quicker to adapt as AI technology changes.

 
 
 

AI in the Wild

 
 
ALEXANDRE MENEGHINI/REUTERS
 

Swiss food giant Nestle wants to use AI to automate its factories. But getting to KitKat production with no human intervention will be no easy task. To start on that path, the company opened a technology facility in Switzerland, and has signed partnerships with Microsoft and robotics company Boston Dynamics. Discussions for further partnerships with Google and Apple are under way.

 
 
 

Other Highlights From the Week in AI

 

• Cisco Systems and OpenAI are working on an open-source software project to protect against AI agent-driven cyberattacks.

 

• Data analytics software company Databricks is in early talks to raise new funds at a $225 billion valuation.

 

• California’s attorney general issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia as part of an investigation focused on its dealings in China and whether it misled investors.
